source: Lieder & Griffiths (2017) Strategy selection as rational metareasoning (Psych Rev; OSF preprint text read)
finding: Strategy selection is cast as a contextual bandit. The value of computation (VOC) of a strategy on a problem is the utility of the action it picks minus the cost of running it. Cost is an opportunity cost: reward rate times execution time. The mind must pick a strategy from perceivable problem features only.
numbers: Formal: VOC(s,p) = E[u(action)] - lambda*E[time]. Goal: learn a map from features f(p) to strategies that maximises expected VOC over the problem distribution.
quote: people learn to predict the accuracy and execution time of each strategy from features of individual problems
limits: Computational-level definition. The set of strategies and the problem features are given to the model, not learned.
agent_relevance: Maps directly to a table of (expected gain - cost) per problem class for the S0 gate. The cost term must be time or tokens, set by what an hour of the agent is worth.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2017) Strategy selection as rational metareasoning (Psych Rev; OSF preprint text read)
finding: The learning rule is a feature-based Bayesian model of each strategy. Two separate linear models are learned per strategy: one predicts execution time, one predicts reward (logistic if binary). They are combined into a VOC estimate. Reward rate is estimated with a Gaussian prior worth 60 seconds of experience. Strategy choice uses Thompson sampling: draw weights from each posterior and pick the argmax VOC.
numbers: Four components: (i) VOC-based choice, (ii) feature-based learning, (iii) separate time and accuracy models, (iv) Thompson-sampling exploration. Prior on reward rate: 60 s of experience. Bayesian model selection also picks which features matter.
limits: Linear predictors only. Authors say the structure resembles semi-gradient SARSA and a small feed-forward net; no claim it is how the brain does it.
agent_relevance: A cheap, code-only implementation: per class keep running mean and variance of success and token cost, sample, pick the best. No model call is needed for the selection step (supports G1, G5, G12).

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2017) Strategy selection as rational metareasoning (Psych Rev; OSF preprint text read)
finding: Experiment 1 (sorting): people choose between cocktail sort and merge sort from list features. After 11 forced-strategy training trials, 83% of people chose merge sort more often when it was the better strategy. Old theories (SSL, RELACS, SCADS) predicted failure; the feature-based model predicted success.
numbers: N=100 MTurk. Merge sort chosen for 81.67% of long nearly-inverted lists (4.9 of 6), but 29.83% of long nearly-sorted lists and 27.00% of short nearly-sorted lists. 83% of participants adaptive (95% credible interval 74.9% to 89.4%). Training median 2.45 errors per list.
limits: MTurk adults following forced step-by-step sort instructions; the strategies are external, not internal. The reported interval [12.9%, 32.4%] around 29.83% is odd in the source text; treat that one interval as unreliable.
agent_relevance: Evidence that strategy choice uses problem features (length times presortedness), including an interaction. An LLM gate must also use combined features, not a single label.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2017) Strategy selection as rational metareasoning (Psych Rev; OSF preprint text read)
finding: Model comparison in Experiment 1. Nine models of earlier theories (SSL, RELACS, SCADS, each with three reward functions) all failed to be adaptive. Rational metareasoning was adaptive in 70.5% of simulated runs; the best SCADS variant (hand-tuned categories, VOC reward) in 59.0%. People (83%) did better than the model (t(298)=2.34, p=0.01). Removing features, or the VOC criterion, broke the model; removing exploration or the separate time/accuracy models did not matter in this task.
numbers: RM 70.5 +/- 3.2% vs people 83.0%; best SCADS 59.0%; SSL and RELACS lower (all p<0.001 versus people).
limits: The experiment was chosen by simulating 104 candidate designs to separate the models, so the discrimination is partly built in. The training set was unbalanced (cocktail sort faster on most training lists), which hurt SSL and SCADS.
agent_relevance: Context-free averaging (which strategy wins on average) fails on mixed problem sets. Our gate must be keyed on class features.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2017) Strategy selection as rational metareasoning (Psych Rev; OSF preprint text read)
finding: Pilot studies that fed the Experiment 1 design measured how long each strategy takes. Participants executed cocktail sort (Pilot 1) or merge sort (Pilot 2) step by step. Sorting time was regressed on counts of comparisons and moves per list. Merge sort comparisons and moves were each slower than cocktail sort ones, so the best choice depends on list length and presortedness.
numbers: 200 MTurk participants, 100 per pilot, 75 cents each, about 15 minutes. Lists 3 to 56 items; 1-20% inversions, 21-80%, 81-100% in equal shares.
limits: Time model is linear in operation counts; gives a per-operation cost, not a per-problem measurement.
agent_relevance: Costs of a strategy can be predicted from counts of its primitive operations. For us: tokens or calls per operator class.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2017) Strategy selection as rational metareasoning (Psych Rev; OSF preprint text read)
finding: Simulation of Payne et al. (1988) risky choice: with time pressure and with high probability dispersion, the model shifts toward fast attribute-based heuristics (LEX, EBA), as people did. The SCADS model always collapsed onto one strategy because its global associations dominated, so its predicted effects were about zero.
numbers: Model: time pressure raised attribute-based processing by 29.69% (t(1998)=9.70, p<1e-15 in the source) and high dispersion by 44.11% (t(1998)=14.41); my reading of which number belongs to which factor follows the order in the text. SCADS effects -0.1% to 0% and 0% to 0.05% (all p>0.49). Ten Payne strategies plus random and skip.
limits: This is a model simulation compared to published results, not a new human experiment. Lesions: features and exploration were needed, separate cost/benefit models were not.
agent_relevance: Time pressure must change the chosen strategy: a token budget should lower the VOC of slow operators in code.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2017) Strategy selection as rational metareasoning (Psych Rev; OSF preprint text read)
finding: Experiment 2: when thinking costs too much, people learn to think less. Four problem types in a casino task with a high reward rate; best play was to skip or pick at random. People engaged less, earned more per second, and chose at random only on the all-great gambles. Reward per decision did not change.
numbers: N=100 MTurk. Engagement fell from 37% (pretest) to 19% (posttest). Information acquisitions fell by about 1.4 per block (95% CI [-1.60,-0.68]); when engaged, 1.1 per block (d=-0.11). Adaptive randomness rose (d=0.67 on all-great trials). Reward rate d=1.00; reward per decision p=0.49.
limits: Authors note the drop could be plain disengagement; Experiment 3 was built to rule that out. People beat the model in the pretest and changed less than the model predicted.
agent_relevance: Agents should be able to learn to skip thinking on low-stakes classes (supports G11, G12) when the opportunity cost is high.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2017) Strategy selection as rational metareasoning (Psych Rev; OSF preprint text read)
finding: Experiment 3: when people think too little, they learn to think more. Low-stakes games first looked not worth the time, then became the only way to earn money. People raised reward rate, slowed down, and engaged with low-stakes problems more often. This separates rational adaptation from general disengagement.
numbers: N=201 recruited; 57 excluded (28.36%) by an attention check, 144 analysed. Reward rate up (t(143)=2.87, p=0.002, d=0.26). Low-stakes reward per decision 1.93 to 2.42 (p=0.03, d=0.16). Engagement on low-stakes 49.1% to 58.95% (chi2=26.9, p<0.001). Acquisitions on low-stakes 4.97 to 6.42 per trial (p<0.001).
limits: Small effects (d about 0.16 to 0.26). Large exclusion rate (28%). No preregistration seen in the text read.
agent_relevance: Learned strategy selection can raise effort when effort pays: the gate must move both ways, not only toward cheaper modes.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2017) Strategy selection as rational metareasoning (Psych Rev; OSF preprint text read)
finding: Experiment 4: in a mixed environment where half the trials are compensatory and half non-compensatory, always using one strategy gives chance. People still chose the right strategy per trial and improved with practice. Context-free selection (SSL, RELACS) stays at chance; feature-based selection beats chance.
numbers: N=100 MTurk, 100 trials each. Agreement with the correct strategy 76.2% (99% HPD 75.1% to 77.3%), 70.4% in first 10 trials to 80.4% in last 10 (p<0.001). 73% correct already on trial 1. Predictive validities 95% down to 83% (reliable) vs 63% down to 51% (unreliable).
limits: Authors warn this is not definitive: one general strategy might do well on both problem kinds. Above-chance on trial 1 suggests prior expertise. People beat every model.
agent_relevance: Prior knowledge matters: an LLM already knows some cues, so the gate should start from a prior and update, not start blank.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2017) Strategy selection as rational metareasoning (Psych Rev; OSF preprint text read)
finding: Fit to Rieskamp & Otto (2006): the simple SSL reinforcement model fit the human data better than rational metareasoning. This is a loss for the theory on quantitative fit. Authors say the comparison depends on assuming people only have TTB and WADD.
numbers: 168 choices per person in 7 blocks of 24. SSL BIC 60.70 vs RM 68.94; MSE 0.0018 vs 0.0043. SCADS BICs 61.09, 62.38, 62.01. Compensatory only: SSL 32.64 vs RM 34.29; non-compensatory 36.22 vs 37.81. Metareasoning without features had BIC 70.52 (close to full RM).
limits: Fixed two-strategy repertoire; the authors lean on qualitative predictions instead. In that task the explicit validities made features uninformative, so context-free learning is enough.
agent_relevance: Do not over-engineer: when the environment is homogeneous, a plain per-strategy running average is as good as a feature model.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2017) Strategy selection as rational metareasoning (Psych Rev; OSF preprint text read)
finding: Simulation of children's addition strategy development (Siegler & Shipley; Shrager & Siegler SCADS). Rational metareasoning reproduces gradual use of Min and Retrieval strategies and the boost from challenge problems. Lesions: without exploration, new strategies were never tried; without features, the model jumped straight from Sum to Retrieval; accuracy-only reward never found Min.
numbers: Min strategy share rose from 37.2% in the first 50 trials after discovery toward 100%; Min use correlated with sum (r=0.30) and addend difference (r=0.24) over 141,609 simulated trials; challenge problems sped up transfer (Bonferroni 0.05/20).
limits: Qualitative match to published curves, not new child data. Strategy discovery is not modelled; strategies are given. SCADS fit about equally well.
agent_relevance: Exploration is required, or new operators never get tried. Cost-aware reward is required, or cheap operators are never chosen.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2017) Strategy selection as rational metareasoning (Psych Rev; OSF preprint text read)
finding: Authors list what the model does not do: it does not discover new strategies, it presupposes domain-specific features, it assumes a fixed strategy set, it ignores working-memory cost of strategies, and it leaves the exploration mechanism open (Thompson, UCB, epsilon-greedy are all candidates). It also cannot yet tell model-free VOC learning from separate time/accuracy models.
numbers: No numbers. Cites Milli, Lieder & Griffiths (2017): choosing among a small number of strategies is optimal for bounded agents.
limits: These are the stated open problems of the 2017 paper; later work (BMPS, strategy discovery) addresses some.
agent_relevance: Suggests keeping the operator set small and explicit. Feature design for our classes is on us.

source: Lieder, Plunkett, Hamrick, Russell, Hay, Griffiths (2014) Algorithm selection by rational metareasoning as a model of human strategy selection (NIPS)
finding: First formal version: rational metareasoning applied to sorting-algorithm selection. It beat the best published sorting-selection method of the time at choosing the fastest algorithm.
numbers: Versus Guo's decision tree: 99.78% [99.7,99.9] vs 98.5% on Dsort5 test set (p<1e-15); nearly sorted 99.99% vs 99.4%; inversely sorted 83.37% vs 77.0%; random permutations 99.99% vs 85.3%.
limits: Only sorting; authors call it a lower bound for harder problems (combinatorial optimisation, planning). Heavy-tailed runtimes not covered.
agent_relevance: A learned feature-based selector can beat hand-built decision rules, in a setting where the answer is checkable (a timer).

source: Lieder, Plunkett, Hamrick, Russell, Hay, Griffiths (2014) Algorithm selection by rational metareasoning as a model of human strategy selection (NIPS)
finding: Versus the recursive method of Lagoudakis et al.: the metareasoning selector sorted 21 test sets much faster, and still won when limited to the same algorithms.
numbers: 102.5 +/- 0.83 s vs 27.96 +/- 0.02 s (p<1e-15); restricted to the same algorithms 47.90 +/- 0.02 s, still faster.
limits: Speed measured on the authors' own system; the Lagoudakis rule was recomputed for it.
agent_relevance: Exploiting an input feature (presortedness) that a length-only rule ignores is where the gain comes from.

source: Lieder, Plunkett, Hamrick, Russell, Hay, Griffiths (2014) Algorithm selection by rational metareasoning as a model of human strategy selection (NIPS)
finding: Against nine psychological strategy-selection models on seven sorting algorithms, rational metareasoning reached most of the best possible speed; none of the others reached a third. Selection time was counted in the total sorting time, so metareasoning overhead was paid for.
numbers: 88.1 +/- 0.7% of maximal sorting speed vs at most 30% for any of nine alternatives (insertion, selection, bubble, shell, heap, merge, quick sorts).
limits: Simulation on generated lists; the psychological models were not built for 7-way choice.
agent_relevance: Overhead of the selector is counted in the score (G7): the selector must pay for itself.

source: Lieder, Plunkett, Hamrick, Russell, Hay, Griffiths (2014) Algorithm selection by rational metareasoning as a model of human strategy selection (NIPS)
finding: Human test in the NIPS paper (same design as Experiment 1 above): 83% of 100 participants chose merge sort more often when it was superior; the three older theories predicted otherwise.
numbers: 83% adaptive, 95% interval 74.9% to 89.4%; p<1e-11 versus no feature use. Task time 24.7 +/- 6.7 minutes.
limits: Same MTurk sample and design as the journal version; counts as one experiment, not two.
agent_relevance: Same as a03; do not double count.

source: Lieder, Shenhav, Musslick, Griffiths (2018) Rational metareasoning and the plasticity of cognitive control (PLoS Comput Biol)
finding: Learned Value of Control (LVOC): extends strategy selection to continuous control signals. The value of a control signal in a state is a linear function of state features, signal intensity and their interactions, minus cost. Weights are learned by Bayesian regression; selection samples k weight vectors, averages them, and takes the argmax (Thompson-like).
numbers: Eq 6 to 9 in the paper. Compared against Rescorla-Wagner associative learning and Win-Stay Lose-Shift.
limits: Linear value model; control signals are low-dimensional. The paper is a model paper: one attention experiment and four Stroop/Flanker datasets from other labs, no new human data.
agent_relevance: A drop-in recipe for learning which cost-bearing action to apply from state features, with exploration.

source: Lieder, Shenhav, Musslick, Griffiths (2018) Rational metareasoning and the plasticity of cognitive control (PLoS Comput Biol)
finding: LVOC fits the visual-search learning data of Lin et al. (2016) far better than two simple learners, with no parameters fitted to those data.
numbers: BIC: LVOC 1817.8 vs Rescorla-Wagner 9763.2 vs Win-Stay Lose-Shift 3449.9. Rescorla-Wagner learning rate 0.0927.
limits: Fits published group-level curves; the model learns gradually but people unlearn quickly in the test block (authors say it needs change detection).
agent_relevance: Win-stay-lose-shift (the obvious cheap rule) loses badly to feature-based value learning.

source: Lieder, Shenhav, Musslick, Griffiths (2018) Rational metareasoning and the plasticity of cognitive control (PLoS Comput Biol)
finding: LVOC fits reward-driven control in Stroop and Flanker tasks better than the rivals; but it under-predicts the size of an effect.
numbers: Krebs et al.: BIC LVOC 45.3 vs RW 1333.9 vs WSLS 2454.8. Braem et al.: MSE 1.35 (LVOC) vs 3.33 (RW) vs 19.4 (WSLS); predicted conflict-adaptation gap 7 ms vs observed 27 ms. Simulated t(959998)=-164.7 shows p-values from simulated N are meaningless.
limits: Quantitative effect underestimated about 4x; simulations with huge N inflate significance.
agent_relevance: Weak size match: treat predicted gains as direction, not magnitude.

source: Callaway, Gul, Krueger, Griffiths, Lieder (2018) Learning to select computations (UAI; arXiv 1711.06892)
finding: Bayesian metalevel policy search (BMPS): a metareasoning policy built from three features: myopic value of information (VOI1), value of perfect information (VPI) and cost of computation. A linear mix of these explains the value of computation and is cheap to learn.
numbers: Regression on VOI1, VPI and cost explains 90.8% to 100% of variance in the value of computation. At cost 0.001 weights are 0.76*VPI + 0.46*VOI1 - 4.5*cost; at cost 0.1 and above 0.00*VPI + 1.00*VOI1 - 1.00*cost.
limits: Needs an exact model of the agent's own belief updates (a metalevel MDP). VPI by exact integration grows exponentially with model size.
agent_relevance: Gives a principled stopping rule: stop thinking when the best expected value of more computation is below its cost.

source: Callaway, Gul, Krueger, Griffiths, Lieder (2018) Learning to select computations (UAI; arXiv 1711.06892)
finding: BMPS reaches near-optimal metareasoning on three problems and beats meta-greedy and DQN, learning fast.
numbers: Bernoulli bandit: at most 5.19% below optimal; 6.78% to 35.8% better than meta-greedy, 20.3% on average. Planning tree: 99.1% of optimal (0.6535 vs 0.6596) vs meta-greedy 0.60, full deliberation 0.20, DQN 0.58; blinkered approximation 0.6559; heights 2 and 3: 98.4% of optimal. Learned in under 10 iterations with fewer than 20% of the DQN episodes.
limits: Synthetic metalevel MDPs and a hypothetical emergency-management case, no human data. Training cost is paid offline and must be amortised.
agent_relevance: Evidence that the stop-or-continue decision can be learned from three scalar features instead of a heavy policy; a candidate for the impasse detector.

source: Lieder, Griffiths, Huys, Goodman (2018) The anchoring bias reflects rational use of cognitive resources (Psychon Bull Rev)
finding: Resource-rational analysis recipe applied to numerical estimation: define the function (infer the quantity), assume an architecture (a few MCMC-like adjustment steps), derive the optimal number of steps from time cost versus error cost. The optimum is small, so a bias toward the anchor remains. One principle explains ten anchoring phenomena, including why incentives help for self-generated anchors.
numbers: Bias after a fixed number of adjustments decays geometrically with number of steps and grows linearly with anchor-to-truth distance. Table 1 lists ten phenomena (provided and self-generated anchors, uncertainty, knowledge, load, time pressure, alcohol, incentives).
limits: Theory plus simulations of published studies. The model is run on priors elicited from the authors' own confidence intervals for each quantity.
agent_relevance: A worked example of a bias as the output of an optimal stopping rule. For us: stopping early on easy problems is rational, not a defect.

source: Lieder, Griffiths, Huys, Goodman (2018) Empirical evidence for resource-rational anchoring and adjustment (Psychon Bull Rev)
finding: Experiment 1, self-generated anchors (bus-delay prediction): higher time cost shrank adjustment; higher error cost grew it, as the theory predicts.
numbers: N=30 recruited on MTurk, 6 excluded for failing task-understanding questions. Relative adjustment 50.7% to 31.0% with time cost (F(1,69)=21.86, p<0.0001); 31.6% to 50.1% with error cost (F(1,69)=19.49, p<0.0001); interaction n.s. Mean adjustment about 41.3% of the way to the truth (95% CI 38.52 to 44.04).
limits: Small sample; synthetic bus-schedule task with controlled knowledge; unclear whether anchors were truly self-generated (hence Experiment 2).
agent_relevance: Direct test that people trade effort for accuracy by incentive: a small-N test of the cost-benefit core.

source: Lieder, Griffiths, Huys, Goodman (2018) Empirical evidence for resource-rational anchoring and adjustment (Psychon Bull Rev)
finding: Experiment 2, provided anchors: same cost effects. This contradicts Epley & Gilovich (2006), who found incentives did not reduce bias for provided anchors, and agrees with Simmons et al. (2010).
numbers: N=60 recruited, 16 excluded; 74.8% of anchor questions answered correctly. Time cost cut relative adjustment 37.2% to 28.2% (F(1,297)=15.5, p=0.0001); error cost raised it 31.2% to 34.2% (F(1,297)=10.39, p=0.0014). Mean adjustment 29.86% (low anchor) and 27.25% (high anchor).
limits: Error cost effect is only 3 points; effects weaker with the high anchor; adjustments smaller than with self-generated anchors. Alternative explanations (selective accessibility) not excluded.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: effects of incentive on effort are real but modest; do not expect large swings from small cost changes.

source: Callaway, van Opheusden, Gul, Das, Krueger, Griffiths, Lieder (2022) Rational use of cognitive resources in human planning (Nat Hum Behav; preprint text read)
finding: Experiment 1 (Mouselab-MDP planning): people plan close to the best reward-per-click tradeoff, and a rational planning model fit as well or better than named heuristics.
numbers: N=104 Prolific (6+3 excluded). Participants earned 0.92 fewer points than the best possible for their click count; 4.94 more than random (95% CI 4.43 to 5.44). Expanded a path with maximal expected value on 81.5% of clicks (CI 79.6 to 83.3). Best fit: optimal model 45 participants vs best-first search 41 vs 9 other; optimal beat best-first in total likelihood (LL>1250). Stopping: weight on best-vs-next gap 1.68 for people vs 4.64 for the optimal model.
limits: Externalised planning (clicking) may alter the process; small state spaces; best-first was near-optimal here, so the two models are hard to tell apart.
agent_relevance: Planning effort should follow a cost-dependent stop rule that depends on best value and on the gap to the second-best; people under-use the gap.

source: Callaway, van Opheusden, Gul, Das, Krueger, Griffiths, Lieder (2022) Rational use of cognitive resources in human planning (Nat Hum Behav; preprint text read)
finding: Experiment 2: people switch search style when the environment's payoff structure changes. The classical algorithm that is near-optimal in each environment best predicted behaviour there; only the optimal model fit all three.
numbers: N=313 recruited, 298 analysed. Optimal model beat heuristic models in increasing variance (LL=606) and decreasing variance (LL=1276) conditions; best-first with best-vs-next rule fit best in the constant condition (optimal worse by LL=2150). Environments favoured depth-first, breadth-first, best-first respectively.
limits: Optimal model not best in the constant condition. Authors report systematic deviations (forward-search bias, under-sensitivity to relative value).
agent_relevance: Strategy depends on environment: the same agent should search depth-first or breadth-first by problem class, learned from payoff structure.

source: Callaway, van Opheusden, Gul, Das, Krueger, Griffiths, Lieder (2022) Rational use of cognitive resources in human planning (Nat Hum Behav; preprint text read)
finding: Experiments 3 and 4 and limits: people default to forward search even when not required, but switch to backward search when the environment makes it worthwhile. Authors give four limits: externalised planning, small unstructured state spaces, no process-level theory of how people approximate the optimum, and untested working-memory limits.
numbers: Experiment 4: participants looked up a city without a revealed parent only 7.2% of the time; in the constant-variance condition 92.4% of lookups followed revealed parents vs 75.5% in noise-free optimal simulations.
limits: Optimal model is derived for tiny trees; no claim about large real-world planning.
agent_relevance: Habitual defaults (forward search) can be mildly suboptimal; a gate with learned defaults will show the same pattern.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut, Griffiths (2025) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models (arXiv 2410.05563v3)
finding: RaM trains an LLM with a value-of-computation reward inside expert iteration, so it reasons only as much as needed. It cuts generated tokens 23 to 45% across three models while keeping or raising accuracy against few-shot chain of thought and STaR.
numbers: Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B and instruct variants. One reported row: STaR 61.9% / 215.1 output tokens vs RaM 63.5% / 146.2; another: STaR 47.4% / 222.7 vs RaM 50.1% / 170.8; CoT few-shot 56.4% / 253.6 (row-to-model mapping is unclear in my text extraction).
limits: Training-based, the opposite of our no-training rule. Only datasets with verifiable answers; not tested in agentic settings; PPO or DPO versions untested. Preprint under review.
agent_relevance: Shows the VOC idea works as a reward for LLM reasoning length. For a scaffold: use VOC to decide in code when to call extra reasoning.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut, Griffiths (2025) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models (arXiv 2410.05563v3)
finding: RaM makes length depend on difficulty: easy problems get shorter chains than hard ones, and the gap grows. It also generalises out of distribution.
numbers: Hard-vs-easy length reduction: up to 50.3% (RaM) vs 34.4% (STaR) vs 19.0% (CoT few-shot) on one table. Out of distribution (MMLU-CF) 28% to 36% fewer tokens than STaR with similar accuracy.
limits: Knowledge-heavy tasks get larger cuts, math and logic smaller; the difficulty split is by dataset, not per item.
agent_relevance: Supports G12: spending by difficulty is learnable. A per-item difficulty signal still has to come from a cheap code check.

source: Nobandegani, da Silva Castanheira, Otto, Shultz (2018) Over-representation of extreme events in decision-making: a rational metacognitive account (arXiv 1801.09848)
finding: An extension, not by Lieder: when the number of mental samples s depends on the time available, the best importance distribution over outcomes depends on s. The earlier Lieder et al. account gave a rule that ignored s. With few samples (s=2) the model reproduces the fourfold pattern of risk preferences.
numbers: Lieder rule: q(o) proportional to p(o)|u(o)-E[u]|, independent of sample count. New model: q depends on s; s=2 gives the fourfold pattern in outcome probability and magnitude.
limits: I wanted the Lieder, Griffiths and Hsu paper of similar title; this arXiv id is the McGill paper instead, and I did not open the Lieder one. Simulation plus a small empirical check.
agent_relevance: Sampling strategy should depend on the budget: with a tight budget, bias the samples toward extreme cases. Candidate for the generate step.

source: Becker, Lieder et al. (2022) Boosting human decision-making with AI-generated decision aids (Comput Brain Behav)
finding: Optimal strategies found by metareasoning methods were turned into plain-language step lists and tested on people. Procedural instructions were easier to follow than the earlier static descriptions, and the aids improved planning a road trip and choosing a mortgage.
numbers: Experiment 1 control group N=60; Experiment 2 control group 54 participants; mean click agreement with the instructed strategy 68.8% (median 59.8%) in the first experiment.
limits: I read the abstract and parts of the method, not all results tables; exact effect sizes for Experiment 2 not recorded. Task-specific, small samples.
agent_relevance: Learned strategies can be compiled into short instructions: a way to hand the gate's decision to the model as a one-line plan.

source: Rieskamp & Otto (2006) SSL: A theory of how people learn to select strategies (J Exp Psychol Gen)
finding: Source of the strategy selection learning (SSL) model: people learn the average payoff of each strategy in an environment. Described only through Lieder & Griffiths (2017). In a 168-trial investment task, people learned take-the-best in non-compensatory environments and weighted-additive in compensatory ones.
numbers: 168 decisions, two conditions; per Lieder & Griffiths.
limits: Not opened. Numbers come from a secondary description.
agent_relevance: The context-free baseline: a running average per operator.

source: Payne, Bettman, Johnson (1988) Adaptive strategy selection in decision making (J Exp Psychol: LMC)
finding: Showed that people use fast heuristics under time pressure and when probabilities fall off quickly, and slower accurate rules otherwise. Basis for the cost-benefit view of strategy selection.
numbers: No numbers recorded; see simulation in a06.
limits: Not opened; description from Lieder & Griffiths (2017).
agent_relevance: Existing human evidence that strategy shifts with time pressure and problem structure.

source: Russell & Wefald (1991) Do the right thing: studies in limited rationality
finding: Original rational metareasoning: choose computations by their expected value of computation (benefit in decision quality minus cost of time). Intractable in general (Hay et al. 2012), hence myopic and learned approximations.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Not opened; cited in several opened papers (Lieder & Griffiths 2017; Callaway et al. 2018).
agent_relevance: Theoretical root for the S0 gate and stopping rule.

source: Shrager & Siegler (1998) SCADS; Siegler (1996) overlapping waves
finding: SCADS learns associations between problem categories and strategies, plus a global strategy association. It needs problems to be pre-labelled with categories, and the global association can swamp category-specific ones.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Not opened; described through Lieder & Griffiths (2017), who report the global-association flaw in their simulations.
